cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-21-christ.summary: This crowded drawing illustrates the psalm that Christ quoted on the cross, 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?'. Its lower part shows the psalmist in a sarcophagus amid bulls, dogs and lions, an empty cross with the instruments of the Passion, and men casting lots for a garment; above, a bust of the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos among angels, sun and moon blesses the congregation. Christ is thus present both in the prophecy of the Passion and in glory.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
The psalter was made in or near Reims, probably under Archbishop Ebbo (816–835); some scholars argue for a date around 850 under his successor Hincmar.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-21-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:monumental-san-lorenzo-triumphal-arc.summary: Above the arch of the 6th-century basilica, Christ sits on a blue globe at the centre, holding a cross-staff and raising his hand, flanked by Peter, Lawrence and Pope Pelagius II with a model of his church on one side, and Paul, Stephen and Hippolytus on the other; the jewelled cities of Bethlehem and Jerusalem fill the corners. The mosaic marks Pelagius's rebuilding of the shrine over Saint Lawrence's tomb.
facts: Pope Pelagius II built a church over Saint Lawrence's tomb in the 580s; in the 13th century Honorius III built a new church in front of it, and the old triumphal arch now faces into the later choir.
Pelagius II, who holds the model of the church, died of plague in 590 and was succeeded by Gregory the Great.

walters:W.44.22V.summary: Christ, stripped to a loincloth and bound with his hands crossed before a slender red column, stands calm and cross-nimbed between two tormentors who swing their scourges above their heads. The gold ground and the column, which divides his body almost in two, isolate him in the centre of the page. The image invites the reader to linger over the suffering Christ before turning to the Crucifixion on the facing leaf.
facts: This full-page miniature is one of the ten 14th-century additions that form a prefatory picture cycle in Walters W.44.
It faces the Crucifixion (fol. 23r), forming one of the cycle's paired openings.
Fourteenth-century additions to the book indicate that it continued to be used by female owners well after its creation.

walters:W.44.22V.notes: The Walters online record dates this leaf with the whole manuscript to the third quarter of the 13th century, but the Walters' own manuscript description (TEI, The Digital Walters) states that the ten full-page miniatures of the prefatory cycle (fols. 18v–27r) were added in the fourteenth century; the date is corrected accordingly. The worklist year (750) was a parsing error.
